authors: Kris Otteman, Linda Fielder, Emily Lewis
title: A professional imperative: teaching tomorrow's veterinarians to confidently identify and report animal cruelty
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA)
abstract: [No abstract available on PubMed.] Commentary/viewpoint published in JAVMA, Feb 1 2025; 263(2):273. Consistent with the verified title and metadata, the piece frames the identification and reporting of animal cruelty as a professional and ethical imperative for veterinarians and calls on veterinary educators to prepare graduates to confidently recognize, document, and report suspected animal cruelty.
takeaways: Recognizing and reporting animal cruelty is positioned as a core professional/ethical duty; shelter and forensic veterinarians should be trained to identify, document, and report suspected cruelty. Relevant to ABVP welfare, forensics, and public-policy content.

authors: Lena DeTar, Jaclyn Bubnell, M Erin Henry, Daniel Lopez, Jessica Reed
title: When goals align: targeted trap-neuter-(vaccinate)-return project helps students, shelters, cats, and communities
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA)
abstract: In 2024, Cornell University's Maddie's Shelter Medicine Program, in collaboration with the College of Veterinary Medicine and the local society for the prevention of cruelty to animals (SPCA), launched a service-learning, high-volume trap-neuter-(vaccinate)-return (TNR) initiative at the request of local neighborhood residents to address a chronic community cat crisis and provide needed surgical opportunities for veterinary students. This mixed-methods study investigated the short-term impacts of the project on student surgical experiences, shelter metrics, and community perceptions of human and feline well-being. Through observational and prospective quantitative and qualitative methods, the researchers analyzed changes in student surgical opportunity, shelter cat metrics, and caregiver experiences before and after the 2024 project. During 2024, 147 cats underwent TNR and 48 participating students increased their on-site surgical volume by approximately 3 procedures. Qualitative feedback revealed gains in confidence and perception of professional readiness. Shelter data showed a moderate impact compared to other TNR studies; benefits included a significant reduction in unweaned kittens and a 3-fold reduction in euthanasia from the target community (OR, 3.89; 95% CI, 1.55 to 9.8). A small increase in intake from this neighborhood after intervention reflected better alignment between community needs (fewer) and access to shelter services (more). The largest impact of the project was in the community. Residents reported profound improvements in cat welfare, kitten births, and mortality. They also reported reduced fighting, injuries, and property damage and renewed trust in the local society for the prevention of cruelty to animals. This mixed-methods study demonstrated that a collaborative, service-learning, large-scale TNR intervention generated meaningful benefits for the target community, the local shelter, cats, and veterinary students.
takeaways: Targeted, high-volume TNVR produced a 3-fold reduction in euthanasia (OR 3.89) and fewer unweaned kittens from the target community while improving resident-reported cat welfare and trust; the service-learning model also boosted student surgical volume and confidence. Supports targeted community-cat sterilization as an effective population-management and access-to-care strategy.

authors: Lena DeTar, Kyrsten Jade Janke, Linda Jacobson
title: Randomized, non-inferiority clinical trial of three topical dermatophytosis treatments in shelter cats
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: Objectives: Topical treatments, along with systemic oral antifungals, are the mainstay of infection and environmental control for cats with dermatophytosis in animal shelters. This study aimed to provide realistic expectations of the performance of three commonly used topical treatments to help shelters minimize the length of stay and optimize feline welfare. Methods: A prospective, randomized, semi-blinded clinical trial compared treatment success and time to cure for miconazole chlorhexidine (MC) and hydrogen peroxide (HP) shampoos vs lime sulfur (LS) using a non-inferiority model. Cats with Microsporum canis were enrolled at four US animal shelters, treated with oral itraconazole and randomized into three topical treatment groups. Treatment success was defined as mycological cure by 7 weeks, while inferiority was defined as requiring more than 1 additional week to achieve cure. Results: A total of 76 cats were enrolled. LS significantly outperformed both alternatives in cure by 7 weeks. Time to cure analysis showed significant differences between LS (mean 27 days, range 7-45) vs MC (37, 14-62) (P = 0.04) and LS vs HP (36, 11-65) (P = 0.06). Although alternative products took significantly longer to cure, confidence intervals (CIs) around the difference of means included the inferiority margin: LS vs MC (9.66, 95% CI 0.7-18.5) and LS vs HP (8.54, 95% CI 0.44-16.6). Therefore, inferiority of the alternative products was suggestive but inconclusive. After controlling for confounders, a Cox proportional hazards analysis confirmed significantly poorer performance of MC (P = 0.003) and HP (P = 0.032) vs LS. Younger age also significantly prolonged treatment (P = 0.039), while intake type, co-housing and low body condition score did not. Shelter staff ratings showed no differences between products in terms of treatment unpleasantness, difficulty or cat reactions. Conclusions and relevance: In this study, LS outperformed HP and MC in treating cats with M canis. Younger cats took a longer time to achieve cure. If shelters or practitioners wish to use an alternative topical treatment to LS, then HP should be considered.
takeaways: Lime sulfur remained the most effective topical adjunct (alongside oral itraconazole) for M. canis dermatophytosis in shelter cats, outperforming miconazole-chlorhexidine and hydrogen peroxide shampoos; younger cats took longer to cure. If an alternative to lime sulfur is needed, hydrogen peroxide is the better second choice.

authors: Aimee M Dalrymple, Lena G DeTar, Jennifer Weisent, Rachael E Kreisler
title: Shelter Medicine Programs Support Multiple AAVMC Competency Domains: A Survey of Shelter Medicine Programming at AVMA-Accredited Colleges
abstract: Shelter medicine is a veterinary specialty that intersects with primary care, community practice, and animal welfare. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the availability of formal (for-credit) education in shelter medicine at American Veterinary Medical Association-accredited colleges of veterinary medicine (CVMs). A 24-question survey, available from July to September 2023, was distributed to targeted faculty members at each CVM. A total of 43 of 54 colleges responded (80%). Formal education in shelter medicine was offered by 38 (88%) institutions. The median shelter medicine program starting year was 2012 (interquartile range [IQR] 2007-2017) and program duration was a median of 12 years (IQR 6-16). The median number of Association of American Veterinary Medical Colleges competency domains addressed through shelter medicine program instruction in colleges with formal shelter medicine education was 7/9 (IQR 4-8); the mode was 9/9. Responding institutions employed 118 shelter medicine faculty and instructors with a median of two shelter medicine faculty members (IQR 2-4) employed per college. In total, 30 instructors were adjuncts (25%), and only 6 of 118 (5%) were tenured. Nine of the 43 CVMs (21%) indicated that the shelter medicine program had been discontinued at some point. Lack of faculty (5/9; 56%) was the most commonly stated reason, followed by lack of a relationship with a shelter (4/9; 44%). Program instability may also be related to factors unique to shelter medicine programs, including increased faculty effort required to secure and maintain funding and community partnerships, competing demands of funders and program stakeholders, and a low proportion of tenured, boarded and permanent faculty.
takeaways: Formal shelter medicine education is widespread (88% of responding AVMA-accredited colleges) and addresses a median 7/9 AAVMC competency domains, but programs are vulnerable to instability from low faculty tenure (only 5% tenured) and dependence on external funding and shelter partnerships. Demonstrates shelter medicine's broad role in veterinary curricula.

authors: Lena G DeTar, Savannah M Martin
title: Microwave radiation injuries in a 7-week-old kitten: a case report
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association (JAVMA)
abstract: [No abstract available on PubMed.] Case report published in JAVMA 2025; 263(5):1-5 (doi:10.2460/javma.24.11.0715). PubMed-listed subject keywords for the article are: burn management; forensics; maltreatment; microwave radiation; shelter medicine.
takeaways: Microwave radiation produces a distinctive thermal-injury/burn pattern relevant to non-accidental injury and animal-maltreatment investigations; shelter and forensic veterinarians should recognize, document, and manage such burns. Relevant to ABVP forensics/cruelty and burn-management content.

authors: Bruce G Kornreich, Diego G Diel, Lena G Detar, Elisha A Frye, Laura B Goodman, Gary R Whittaker
title: Feline health center initiative to track avian flu spread in cats
abstract: [No abstract available on PubMed.] This American Journal of Veterinary Research item (PMID 42248198) describes the Cornell Feline Health Center (CFHC) Feline H5N1 Surveillance Consortium, an interdisciplinary initiative (including shelter medicine, virology, diagnostics, and public-health expertise; Dr. Lena DeTar is the associate clinical professor of shelter medicine on the team) launching a pilot surveillance program that tests cats at shelters, clinics, and veterinary hospitals in New York state. As verified through Cornell University sources, H5N1 avian influenza causes severe disease in cats with mortality up to roughly 70%, yet little is known about feline-to-feline transmission, whether cats act as a vector to other animals or humans, or how common infection is in community cat populations; the consortium aims to answer these questions.
takeaways: H5N1 (HPAI) is an emerging, often-fatal (up to ~70% mortality) infection in cats with zoonotic/one-health implications, and shelters are a key surveillance setting for early detection. Relevant to ABVP infectious disease and community/public-health domains.
